body.p: This important study presents a high-throughput pipeline for characterizing the home-cage behavior and vocalizations of marmosets, applied to a large colony (5,400 sessions from 120 animals in 36 families). The authors show that behavior varies widely from day to day, tracking the behavior of cagemates and the call rate in the housing room. A subset of stimuli (reward tablet, intruder, mask, treat) elicits strong and consistent responses. Combinations of baseline and stimulus-response features are stable within animals across months and are partly shared within families. The evidence for the descriptive results is convincing. The dataset and pipeline will be of value to groups developing marmoset models of brain disorders and to the computational ethology community.

[Editor's note: this version has been assessed by the Reviewing Editor without further input from the original reviewers. The authors have addressed the comments raised in the previous round of review.]
Summary:
The authors demonstrate a fully unsupervised, high throughput (meaning very low human interaction required) approach to quantifying marmoset behavior in unconstrained environments.
Strengths:

The authors provide an approach that is scalable, easy to implement at face value, and highly robust. Currently, most behavioral quantification approaches do not work well on marmosets, or the published examples that do look promising do not scale towards high throughput as demonstrated by the authors.

While marmosets can certainly be a useful translational research model devoid of free behavior quantification, the authors make a compelling point about how this approach can be useful in the study of treatments of emerging marmoset disease models.
Overall this is a very exhaustive manuscript that overcomes significant shortcomings in previous work and speaks highly to the use of marmosets for unconstrained behavioral and neural assessment.
Weaknesses:

Recording marmoset behavior with a 60Hz frame rate is a significant limitation to the approach which is hopefully easily alleviated in the future. Marmosets (in the reviewers' experience) have a lot of motion energy above the 30Hz nyquist limit imposed by this system and are agile to a degree requiring higher frame rates.

In this manuscript, Menegas et al. classify the "control" behavior of captive marmosets. They combine behavioral screening from video recordings with audio and neural recordings (from the striatum) to better define what can be considered a typical behavioral repertoire for captive marmoset monkeys. A range of analyses is presented, investigating various aspects of behavior, such as social interactions and the detection of atypical individuals.
The manuscript is compelling in many respects, especially due to the richness of the dataset and the breadth of analyses presented.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.
We thank the editors and reviewers for their careful reading of our manuscript and their helpful suggestions. We have substantially revised the manuscript. The main changes are:
(1) We removed the term “natural behavior” throughout the manuscript. We now describe the data as behavior recorded in the home cage under laboratory conditions.

(2) We focused the paper more clearly on behavior. The revised Results describe the distribution of behavior in the home cage, how it varies across days, and how it is related to the behavior of cagemates and to the call rate in the room.

(3) We added several new figures and Results sections. Together, they show how consistently animals respond to each stimulus, which behavioral traits are stable across recordings (test-retest consistency), and how these traits are related to stimulus responses and to the behavior of cagemates.

(4) We removed several elements that were not central to the main logic of the paper, to keep the paper focused and keep its length reasonable. Notably, we removed the neural recordings, the sleep data, and the cognitive testing data.

(5) We substantially expanded the Methods. We added a section related to each type of analysis, information on housing conditions, an ethics statement, a statistical analysis section, and a section on animal and data selection.

(6) We made the source data and the code needed to reproduce every figure panel publicly available on GitHub. We also made the code pipelines used for the core analyses (pose estimation, behavioral state labeling, track filtering, and visualization) publicly available on GitHub and uploaded additional processed data to Zenodo.

disp-quote.p: (1) Recording marmoset behavior with a 60Hz frame rate is a significant limitation to the approach which is hopefully easily alleviated in the future through better cameras/reconstruction pipelines. Marmosets (in the reviewers’ experience) have a lot of motion energy above the 30Hz nyquist limit imposed by this system and are agile to a degree requiring higher frame rates.

body.p: We agree that recording at 60 fps limits our ability to fully resolve the fast movements of marmosets. We chose this frame rate as part of a logistical tradeoff that allowed us to capture broad patterns in behavior from a large number of cages rather than detailed 3D kinematics from a smaller number of cages, based on the resources and level of expertise that we had at the time. We agree that higher-resolution studies are possible, as with OpenMonkeyStudio (Bala, 2020), but we do not have this type of dataset available. We have added a reference to this limitation:

“Notably, our recordings were made at 60 frames per second, which allowed us to collect and store data from a large number of cages. This may be sufficient for behavioral states lasting hundreds of milliseconds or longer, but higher frame rates would be needed to precisely resolve the kinematics of all marmoset movements.”
One additional benefit of having higher-resolution 3D data would be the ability to resolve the facial expressions of animals from side-view cameras.

disp-quote.p: (2) The manuscript neglects recent approaches to non-human primate behavioral quantification from other groups that should be included. Simians are simians after all.

body.p: We agree with this point. We now acknowledge other approaches to tracking and quantifying primate behavior in the manuscript, and we do not claim that our approach is the first, best, or only way to track marmosets. Instead, we focus on looking for broad patterns in the resulting data. Because a relative strength of our study is the large number of animals and recordings, we focus on describing how behavior varies across days, cagemates, and stimuli. In particular, we now focus on describing which traits are stable within individuals and families.

disp-quote.p: (3) As a minor weakness, this reviewer would have liked to see code shared for the reviewers to evaluate, especially pertaining to the high throughput and robustness of the approach.

body.p: We apologize for this. We submitted the paper before organizing the code in a way that would be easily readable and sharable. The data and code to reproduce each figure are now publicly available (https://github.com/williammenegas/Marmoset_Quantification_2026). The behavioral pipeline (marm_behavior), the track-filtering code (marm_filt), and plotting code for the output files (marm_viz) are also now publicly available on GitHub. This approach is robust to new videos from our colony but may require network fine-tuning for videos from other cage types.

disp-quote.p: The manuscript is compelling in many respects, especially due to the richness of the dataset and the breadth of analyses presented. However, a significant issue with the manuscript lies in its writing: the results are conveyed in an overly succinct and superficial manner, and the “Methods” section is nearly absent. Key concepts are often undefined, and the mathematical details underlying the figures are not explained, leaving readers to guess the authors’ approach.

body.p: We agree, and we thank the reviewer for providing the detailed list of examples below. We have rewritten the Results and expanded the Methods. We added Methods sections related to the quantification of state transition structure, the correlation between cagemates, the relationship between call rate and behavior, the comparison of control and stimulus sessions, the creation of stimulus response maps, the test-retest analysis, the process of identifying baseline/stimulus dimensions, and the definition of trait-based groups. We also added a section related to statistical analysis that describes each test, and a section related to animal/data selection that describes which data was used for each type of analysis.

We also hope that uploading the behavioral pipeline (marm_behavior), the track-filtering code (marm_filt), plotting code for the output files (marm_viz), and the source data/code needed to reproduce the figures (https://github.com/williammenegas/Marmoset_Quantification_2026) will help clarify the details of how each type of analysis was performed.

disp-quote.p: Another issue is the vague use of the term “natural behavior.” All data presented here appear to have been collected in small cages with limited climbing opportunities and enrichment. Thus, the authors should refrain from using “natural” to describe these conditions.

body.p: We agree with this assessment. We removed the term “natural behavior” throughout the manuscript. We now describe the data as behavior recorded “in the cage”, “in a laboratory setting”, or “in control sessions”. For example:
“To treat the study of marmoset behavior as a quantitative data science problem [32,33], we collected a large dataset of behavioral data from animals living in a laboratory setting.”
We also added further description of the housing conditions, and how they were modified during the recording periods. For example:
“After these cage modifications, the final size of the area used for the recording was approximately 75 cm x 75 cm x 75 cm.”

disp-quote.p: (1) “we temporarily placed horizontal cage dividers to reduce the total cage size during data collection”: What were the resulting (and initial) cage dimensions?

body.p: We now give the size of the recording area in the Methods. During recordings, a horizontal divider was placed in the middle of the cage, and the cage was restored to its normal state after each session:
“After these cage modifications, the final size of the area used for the recording was approximately 75 cm x 75 cm x 75 cm.”

disp-quote.p: (2) “After training the network, we hierarchically clustered the latent space”: What is the latent space? Based on Figure 2a, it appears related to the network’s recurrent layer, but this is not clarified in the text.

body.p: The latent space is the output of the bottleneck layer of the recurrent network (Fig. 2c). The network used 20 seconds of postural features as input and was trained to predict the next 5 seconds. We used the 256-dimensional bottleneck output at each frame for clustering. We now define this in the Methods:
“This network had a bottleneck layer of 256 units. The latent space was the 256-dimensional output of this bottleneck layer, computed for each frame.”

disp-quote.p: (3) Alpha and perplexity parameters: Please define these terms. Since these concepts appear fundamental, readers should not have to consult external references.

body.p: We now define both parameters in the Methods:

“As suggested in tree-SNE [31], we systematically varied the alpha (exaggeration) and perplexity (number of neighbors) in the t-SNE clustering algorithm. At high levels of alpha/perplexity, we observed fewer distinct clusters. At lower levels of alpha/perplexity, we observed more distinct clusters.”

disp-quote.p: (4) “We then traced cluster identities across hierarchical levels”: What are hierarchical levels?

body.p: Each hierarchical level is one clustering of the latent space. We traced cluster identities between neighboring levels, so that each fine cluster belongs to one cluster at each coarser level (Fig. S3). We now define the levels in the Methods:
We refer to each of these clustering results as a hierarchical level, from level 1 (4 clusters) to level 5 (80 clusters).

disp-quote.p: (5) “To understand how the input time series data was weighed in the bottleneck layer of the model”: What is the bottleneck layer?

body.p: We removed the analysis of how the model’s attention was distributed that was referenced here, because we believe it is beyond the scope of this project to study how the model allocates attention across the input time series. We believe that this could be an interesting project in itself but that it distracted from the main points of this paper. Our goal in this revision is to focus the paper on the behavioral results.

disp-quote.p: (6) “we measured the average attention allocation to previous time points”: The authors should define “attention allocation.”

body.p: We removed this analysis from the revised manuscript, as mentioned above.

disp-quote.p: (7) “we compared each neuron’s firing rate distribution to shuffled data based on the overall frequency of each behavior during the session”: This description is insufficient to understand the analysis.

body.p: We removed this analysis from the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (8) “we hierarchically clustered neurons according to their firing rate enrichment maps”: No mathematical explanation is provided for neuron clustering, nor is the concept of a “firing rate enrichment map” clarified.

body.p: We removed this analysis from the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (9) “Cluster 4 showed higher activity when neurons were ‘alone’ or ‘active’”: This is vague and uses unclear jargon (e.g., “neurons alone”). Additionally, no mathematical explanation is provided for assigning neuronal activity to behavioral states.

body.p: We removed the striatal recordings from this manuscript, because they did not fit the main logic of the paper. We will describe these data fully in a separate paper, which contains data from other recording modalities that will help explain and support those findings.

disp-quote.p: (10) Figure 3f, right-side panels: The analysis seems to involve cage mate positioning, yet no description is provided.

body.p: This figure was part of the neural analysis, which we removed from this manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (11) “we used motion watches to measure activity across all hours”: Are these motion-sensitive watches physically attached to the animals? The methodology should be described, including data analysis details.

body.p: We removed the motion-watch data from the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: “Natural behavior”: Typically, the term “natural” suggests that the dataset reflects the range of behaviors exhibited by animals in the wild. Here, however, recordings were made in a small cage with limited climbing opportunities and enrichment. Under these conditions, it’s hard to justify describing the behavior as “natural”.

body.p: We agree, and we removed the term throughout the manuscript.

disp-quote.p: In a project aimed at classifying the behavioral repertoire of marmoset monkeys and making this dataset accessible to other laboratories, it would be helpful to include more detailed information about the animals’ housing conditions. This might include cage sizes, temperature, humidity, and details on food quantities, quality, and feeding times.

body.p: We have added additional information to the Methods, for example:
“The lights in the facility were turned on at 7:00 am and turned off at 7:00 pm.”
“The facility was maintained at 26 °C and 45 ± 10% relative humidity.”
“After these cage modifications, the final size of the area used for the recording was approximately 75 cm x 75 cm x 75 cm.”
“Food was placed into two bowls that fit into slots designed to hold them so that they remained in place.”

The Methods also describe the timing of veterinary checks and cage changes, and the changes we made to the cage for recording. Importantly, we describe the placement of a transparent ceiling, a horizontal divider, a bed, and two food bowls. We also describe the removal of the ledges and nest boxes during sessions.

disp-quote.p: Correlation versus causation: In the section titled “Large-scale data collection reveals variability across days and correlation between cagemates,” the authors conclude: “Overall, these results indicate that measurements of animals’ behavioral traits depend heavily on their social environment.” This interpretation seems incorrect. We know that animal behavior varies throughout the day, with activity peaks typically occurring in the morning and afternoon. Such factors, or other external influences, could induce correlations between animals that are not caused by social interactions.

body.p: We agree that this sentence overstated our conclusion, and we have rewritten it to be more accurate. We believe that daily rhythms are unlikely to explain the correlation, because each session started at about the same time of day, each value is a fraction of the session, and each value was expressed relative to the colony mean for that session type.
“To normalize this data, we subtracted the colony mean for that session type from each value.”
However, cagemates also share their room and recording schedule, so other external influences could contribute.

“Overall, these results suggest that measurements of animals’ behavioral traits are strongly correlated to their social environment. Because cagemates are recorded in the same room and with the same recording schedule, external factors such as the call rate in the room could also contribute to this correlation.”

disp-quote.p: Figure 4g: What are we intended to conclude from this analysis?

body.p: We removed this panel from the revised manuscript and reworked the figure to be clearer.

disp-quote.p: Figure 5: Please specify the type of calls analyzed. For example, did you analyze only long-distance calls (aka ‘loud phees’ or ‘shrills’)? In “We split the audio data into 5-minute (non-continuous) segments and found that the average call rate in these segments varied from 0 calls per minute to 60 calls per minute (Fig. 5d-e),” does the call rate refer to individual animals or the entire cage?

body.p: The call rate includes calls of all types detected by the call detection network (now Fig. 4b), and not only long-distance calls.
“(b) Example audio data classified by a supervised neural network as containing no calls (top) or calls of any type (bottom).”

The call rate was measured from the microphone beside each cage. Because loud calls could be detected by every microphone in the room, the call rate includes calls from the animals in that cage and loud calls from other cages. It therefore describes the cage, and not individual animals. We now state this more clearly in the Results and in the Statistical analysis section.
“In this setup, all loud calls in the room could be detected by each microphone, and the source could be roughly localized to a single cage.”
“The two animals of a pair shared one call-rate series (68 animals, 35 pairs).”

disp-quote.p: “This implies that a high rate of calls in a room can interrupt animals during social resting states and cause them to preferentially exhibit more active/attentive states.” Does it? This could simply indicate that more active animals produce more calls.

body.p: We agree with this assessment. We softened this statement and added the alternative that the reviewer describes:

“This suggests that a high rate of calls in the room could inhibit social resting and cause animals to preferentially exhibit more active/attentive states. Notably, the animals being measured could also be the source of the calls, themselves. So, this effect could also be related to general arousal (in animals that are both making calls and exhibiting more large movements).”

disp-quote.p: “We recorded neural activity in the striatum because it is known to contain diverse signals related to movement and social interactions.” While I understand that the authors intend to publish neural data separately, a brief discussion of the striatum’s role here would be helpful.

body.p: Because we removed the striatal recordings from this manuscript, we no longer discuss the striatum here. We will describe these data, and the role of the striatum, in a separate paper.
